analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare providers from forcing nurses to work beyond scheduled shifts or 48 hours a week.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2024 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no further action before the 118th Congress ended, so it never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Hospitals and other Medicare providers could no longer make nurses work beyond a scheduled shift, more than 48 hours a week, or more than 12 hours straight, with a required 10-hour rest after a 12-hour shift. Nurses who refuse mandatory overtime or report violations would be protected from firing or retaliation, and facilities could face civil penalties. The rules would not apply during declared emergencies, and nurses could still volunteer for extra hours.
analysis.who_benefits: Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses, especially those routinely pushed into involuntary overtime, plus the patients they care for. Research cited in the bill links long nurse hours to fatigue, impaired vigilance, and medical errors.

how_it_helps.text: Caps mandatory nursing overtime at the scheduled shift, 48 hours per week, or 12 consecutive hours, and requires a 10-hour break after the 12th hour worked.

Protects nurses from being fired, demoted, disciplined, or reported to state licensing boards for refusing mandatory overtime or reporting violations, and sets up a complaint process with the Health and Human Services Secretary.
Lets the Secretary impose civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with stiffer penalties for repeat violators, and publish violators' names online.
The bill's findings note that 18 states have already restricted mandatory overtime for nurses, and that research links regulated nurse work hours to improved patient safety.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and other Medicare-participating providers, which would lose the ability to cover staffing shortages by ordering nurses to stay past their shifts. They would have to hire more staff, rely on voluntary overtime, or pay premiums, and pass those costs to insurers, patients, or taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: In a true staffing shortfall outside a declared emergency, a hospital could no longer require a nurse to stay past a scheduled shift, which could force units to transfer patients, close beds, or delay care until coverage is found.

Hospitals would face new labor costs from hiring additional nurses or paying voluntary-overtime premiums to cover gaps, costs that flow to Medicare, private insurers, and patients in the form of higher payments.

The cap counts on-call and standby time as hours worked even when the nurse is not required to be at the facility, which some providers would argue overstates actual fatigue and limits scheduling flexibility.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is well documented: research cited in the bill ties long, involuntary nurse hours to medical errors and patient harm, and 18 states have already adopted similar limits. The cost is real but ordinary: hospitals would need to staff more predictably rather than absorbing shortages by extending individual nurses' shifts. The main design weakness is that the emergency exception excludes chronic understaffing, so hospitals that run perpetually short would have to fix it rather than paper over it.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Merkley introduced it in March 2024 and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 5, 2024, by Senator Merkley with three Democratic cosponsors (Butler, Van Hollen, and Fetterman).
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill never reached the committee, the floor, or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and other Medicare providers keep the ability to require nurses to work beyond their scheduled shifts without penalty, and nursing staff continue to bear the fatigue and patient-safety risks that the bill cited.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to limit mandatory nurse overtime as a condition of Medicare participation.

for.name: Sens. Laphonza Butler, Chris Van Hollen, and John Fetterman
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction; the bill's only recorded support.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic sponsors (4 senators) and no recorded votes or floor debate, so no partisan split was ever tested.

industries.note: The bill would remove the option of covering staffing gaps by mandating overtime from nurses, forcing providers to hire more staff or pay premiums. Their interest in lower labor costs runs directly against the patient-safety and nurse-fatigue concerns the bill targets.

industries.industry: Nurse staffing agencies and temporary nursing services
industries.note: With mandatory overtime off the table, hospitals facing shortages would need to fill shifts through hires and temporary staffing rather than extending existing nurses' hours, likely increasing demand for agency staffing.
